claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is governed by interface-mediated dislocation nucleation and pile-up.
Severe lattice distortion and compositional complexity enhance local stress concentrations at nanoscale interfaces.
Interface-localized stress concentrations activate multiple slip systems.
Dislocations generated in both FCC and BCC layers accumulate at the interfaces during sustained loading.
Interfacial dislocation accumulation promotes localized shear banding and creep.
The proposed starting coating consists of alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers with sharp interfaces.
The FCC and BCC layers exhibit distinct lattice distortions and compositional fluctuations.
Nanoscale FCC/BCC interfaces restrict conventional dislocation motion.
Nanoscale FCC/BCC interfaces act as sites for dislocation accumulation.
High-entropy-alloy lattice distortions cause preferential dislocation nucleation at interfaces under sustained load.
Interfacial dislocation pile-ups promote eventual slip transmission across layers.
The combined processes of dislocation generation, interfacial blocking, and cross-layer transmission produce progressive creep.
The proposed multilayer has a higher creep rate than refined conventional alloys.
Sustained loading increases dislocation density at or near interfaces relative to the undeformed state.
Sustained loading produces localized shear bands relative to the initially uniform multilayer.
More pronounced interface misfit and lower interfacial bonding strength lead to a higher steady-state creep rate.
Improving interfacial strength lowers creep rate under otherwise identical loading conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the multilayer architecture remains intact and layer coarsening or complete interfacial failure does not occur.
Conventional dislocation mechanisms in metallic multilayers are established.
Chemically enhancing interfacial bonding reduces dislocation pile-up.
